text: Course 3 introduced the basic idea of a collision: the target instance's version of a record differs from the version captured in the Update Set you're promoting. This lesson covers what to actually do about it — the real review workflow, not just the definition.

When ServiceNow flags a collision, it's presenting two competing versions of the same record. The remote update is the incoming change, captured in the Update Set you're promoting. The local update is what's already sitting on the target instance right now. The review screen lets you open both side by side, field by field — and that comparison is the entire point of flagging a collision in the first place.

Once you can see both versions, there are three legitimate outcomes. Keep the remote version, when the incoming change is correct and should overwrite the target. Keep the local version, when someone made a legitimate, intentional change directly on the target for a reason the Update Set doesn't know about. Or reconcile manually, when neither version alone is correct on its own.

The dangerous default is clicking accept remote on every collision without reading the comparison, on the assumption that whatever came from the development pipeline must be right. A collision exists precisely because something changed on the target after the Update Set was created. That change might be a legitimate hotfix. Accepting remote blindly throws that work away silently, and nobody necessarily notices until the thing that was fixed breaks again.

Reconciliation is the right call whenever the two versions touch genuinely different aspects of the same record — say, the remote update changes a script's logic while the local update changes an unrelated field. Picking either side alone would lose real, intentional work from the other side. The fix is combining both sets of changes into one corrected version before the commit finishes.

A collision is never just an obstacle to click past — it's a deliberate checkpoint asking you to compare two real versions and choose, or combine, correctly. Next up: what happens when preview or commit itself runs into trouble, including missing dependencies, skipped records, and partial commits.
